title: Debugging clinic
goal: Find the reason a pandas result is wrong, then repair it.
prerequisites: Modules 1–20; revisit selection, cleaning, and joins.

cells.title: A label is not a row position
cells.explanation: A table can use student IDs as its index. Position 0 still means the first row, but the label of that row is now S001. Read the index before choosing a selector.
cells.code:
df = students().set_index("Student_ID")
by_position = df.iloc[0:2][["Name", "Score"]]
by_label = df.loc["S001":"S002", ["Name", "Score"]]
print(by_position)
print("Same rows:", by_position.equals(by_label))

questions.prompt: What labels does df use now?
questions.answer: The Student_ID values, such as S001, are index labels.

questions.prompt: Why do both selections contain two rows?
questions.answer: iloc excludes stop position 2; loc includes both existing endpoint labels S001 and S002.

questions.prompt: Would df.loc[0] mean the first row here?
questions.answer: No. It asks for label 0, which is absent, so it raises KeyError.

cells.task: Select S003 through S005 by label, then select the same three students by position. Print both and confirm equality.
cells.hint: The first selected row has position 2. The excluded stop must be one position after S005.
cells.solution:
df = students().set_index("Student_ID")
by_label = df.loc["S003":"S005", ["Name", "Score"]]
by_position = df.iloc[2:5][["Name", "Score"]]
print(by_label)
print(by_position)
print("Same rows:", by_label.equals(by_position))
cells.solution_note: Both results contain Chloe, Dana, and Ethan. Labels and positions happen to select the same records here, but they express different rules.

options: The stop in an iloc slice
The stop in every loc label slice
check.feedback: iloc uses Python's stop-exclusive positional slicing. Existing loc slice endpoints are included.

cells.watch: An integer inside loc is a label, even when it looks like a row number.
cells.takeaway: Choose a selector from the meaning of the request, not from habit.

cells.title: Repair a condition with two rules
cells.explanation: A filter must produce one True or False value per row. Combine pandas conditions with & for AND or | for OR, with parentheses around each comparison. The broken expression is a comment so this example can run.
cells.code:
df = students()
# Broken: df[(df["Score"] >= 80) and (df["Attendance"] >= 90)]
mask = (df["Score"] >= 80) & (df["Attendance"] >= 90)
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Score", "Attendance"]]
print(result)

questions.prompt: What does each True in mask represent?
questions.answer: A student meeting both the score and attendance conditions.
Yes. Her score is 82 and attendance is 94.

questions.prompt: Why is and wrong for these Series?
questions.answer: and expects a single truth value. Each comparison returns a Series of truth values, which & combines element by element.

cells.task: Find students whose Score is below 70 OR whose Attendance is below 80. Print their IDs and both values.
cells.hint: Use | and keep both comparisons in parentheses.
cells.solution:
df = students()
mask = (df["Score"] < 70) | (df["Attendance"] < 80)
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Score", "Attendance"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: S004, S008, and S011 meet at least one condition. S011 qualifies by score even though attendance is 82.

check.prompt: A student meets only one of two conditions. Which operator keeps that student?
check.feedback: OR (|) accepts a row when either condition is True; AND (&) requires both.

cells.watch: Do not remove the parentheses around each comparison.
cells.takeaway: Translate AND, OR, and NOT into &, |, and ~.

cells.title: Change the table you actually intend to change
cells.explanation: A filtered table and the original table are different objects. Use a single .loc assignment when the original must change. Use .copy() when creating a separate working table, and inspect both afterward.
cells.code:
df = students()
mask = df["Student_ID"].eq("S004")
# Avoid: df[mask]["Score"] = 70
df.loc[mask, "Score"] = 70
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Score"]]
print(result)

questions.prompt: What score will S004 have now?
Why should you avoid the commented chained assignment?
questions.answer: It writes through an intermediate object. Under pandas Copy-on-Write it cannot update the original DataFrame.

cells.task: Start with a fresh df = students() and create a separate copy of its RAK rows named rak. Add 5 points to scores in rak. Show that Amira's copied score is 93 while her score in df remains 88.
cells.solution:
df = students()
rak = df.loc[df["Campus"].eq("RAK")].copy()
rak["Score"] = rak["Score"] + 5
print("Copied score:", rak.loc[rak["Student_ID"].eq("S001"), "Score"].iloc[0])
print("Original score:", df.loc[df["Student_ID"].eq("S001"), "Score"].iloc[0])
cells.solution_note: The working copy changes; the original data stays available for comparison. For these numeric columns, .copy() makes the intended separation explicit.

check.feedback: Name the target DataFrame and select its rows and columns in one .loc assignment.

cells.watch: A method returning a new object is not an instruction to update the old one.

cells.title: A correct total can still hide a bad merge
cells.explanation: Two tables may contain the same key more than once. Matching repeated keys can multiply records. Validate the intended relationship and inspect unmatched IDs before calculating a report.
cells.code:
left = students()[["Student_ID", "Name"]]
right = assessment()
result = left.merge(right, on="Student_ID", how="outer",
                    validate="one_to_one", indicator=True)
print(result.loc[result["_merge"].ne("both"), ["Student_ID", "_merge"]])
print("Rows:", len(result))

questions.answer: The merge keys must be unique in each input table.
S012 appears only in students; S013 appears only in assessment.

questions.prompt: Why is a left merge alone insufficient to find extra assessment IDs?
questions.answer: It preserves left-side students but discards right-only records, including S013.

cells.task: Keep only enrolled students with a left merge stored in result. Keep the merge indicator column, and store the count of students with no assessment in missing_count.
cells.solution:
result = students().merge(assessment(), on="Student_ID", how="left",
                          validate="one_to_one", indicator=True)
missing_count = result["_merge"].eq("left_only").sum()
print(result[["Student_ID", "Quiz", "_merge"]])
print("Enrolled students without assessment:", missing_count)
cells.solution_note: The result has 12 enrolled students and one missing assessment, S012. The earlier outer audit also exposed S013 for follow-up.

check.prompt: What can a many-to-many merge do?
options: Create multiple matches for each repeated key
check.feedback: Repeated keys match every compatible combination. Check uniqueness and use validate before summarizing.

cells.watch: Do not remove duplicate keys without understanding why they exist.
cells.takeaway: Audit the join before trusting the summary.
